quote: Welche algebraische Zahlen befriedigen lineare Differen- tialgleichungen 1ster und 2ter Ordnung? In meinem[?] d.h. durch Congruenzen bestimmten Sinne.
english: Which algebraic numbers satisfy linear differential equations of 1st and 2nd order? In my sense, i.e. the sense determined by congruences.
topic: The page completes a criterion for continuity via fundamental sequences, then notes research problems on algebraic numbers satisfying linear differential equations, on proving the rationality of Bernoulli numbers from Riemann's zeta integral, and on proving Wiener's assertion about the special Pascal theorem.

triage.modern_statement: I can't pin down a single precise modern statement. Hilbert wants to know which algebraic numbers satisfy first- and second-order linear differential equations, with 'differentiation' defined for numbers 'in my sense, determined by congruences'. The note doesn't say what that sense is, and I found no source that does. One plausible reading: fix a prime p and treat a congruence-based operator, such as the Fermat-quotient p-derivation δx = (φ(x) − x^p)/p, as a 'derivative' acting on numbers. Then ask which algebraic numbers (for example in unramified or ramified extensions of Q_p) satisfy linear equations of order 1 or 2 in δ. This reading is my interpretation, not something the page states.
triage.answered_by: No one I could identify answered Hilbert's question as he posed it. The closest modern framework is Alexandru Buium's theory of 'arithmetic differential equations' (book 2005; papers 1990s–2010s), in which Fermat-quotient operators play the role of derivatives on numbers. Buium does not cite Hilbert's note, so treating his theory as an answer would be speculation.

evidence.claim: Buium's theory is an arithmetic version of ordinary differential equations: derivatives become Fermat-quotient operators and functions become numbers. This is a congruence-based way to 'differentiate' numbers.

Buium's monograph 'Arithmetic Differential Equations' builds the theory of ordinary differential equations with derivations replaced by Fermat-quotient operators. It cites Ihara's work on Fermat quotients and differentiation of numbers.

In this framework, the solutions of the basic equation δx = 0 in the p-adic completion of the maximal unramified extension are 0 and the roots of unity. Buium's survey also says the arithmetic jet spaces of certain ramified rings R[α] are empty for n ≥ 1. That limits which algebraic numbers can carry such a derivation structure at all.
Buium's survey also treats linear arithmetic differential equations, the analogue of linear ODEs.
Manin's survey 'Numbers as functions' presents Buium's p-adic arithmetic differential equations as a way of thinking of numbers as functions satisfying differential equations.
The subject was still producing papers in 2014, for example Buium's 'Transcendental numbers as solutions to arithmetic differential equations'.

triage.why: The question is real research mathematics, but it hinges on a private definition ('in my sense, determined by congruences') that the note never spells out. I found no source that reconstructs it. It is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem, and I found no historical study of this diary entry. The nearest modern idea, Buium's Fermat-quotient arithmetic differential equations (studied by Buium, Manin and others), fits the 'congruence derivative' idea well. Even so, nothing in the sources links it to Hilbert or shows it settles exactly which algebraic numbers satisfy first- or second-order linear equations. So I can't say whether the question was answered. For the same reason I marked 'active_today' as unclear: Buium's area was active through at least the mid-2010s, but I don't know that it is the same problem.
